one_liner: Small-size-tuned AVX2 x86-64 assembly memset and memcpy that beat glibc, Folly and musl on 0-511 byte calls.
what_it_does: Two hand-written AT&T-syntax functions, asm_memset and asm_memcpy (src/memset/impl.S, src/memcpy/impl.S), with the standard memset/memcpy signatures, plus C reference versions, an exhaustive correctness tester, a benchmark driver, an LD_PRELOAD length-histogram tool and a memset proxy shim. The functions are exported under their own names, so you call them directly or alias them; nothing replaces libc automatically. The memset was later upstreamed into Folly as __folly_memset (folly/memset.S, Apache-2.0).
how_it_is_fast: Both routines branch on size class and cover each class with two possibly overlapping unaligned stores (1-4, 4-8, 8-16, 16-32, 32-64 bytes, then three or four 32-byte stores up to 128), so a short call costs a couple of compares and two stores with no loop or tail handling. Memsets above 176 bytes store one unaligned head, then 32-byte-aligned vmovdqa stores unrolled five-wide, then one unaligned tail; larger memcpys run a 128-byte loop of four unaligned ymm loads/stores and finish with up to three 32-byte copies plus an overlapping last word. The design follows Joe Bialek's MSRC write-up on Windows memset and targets the short-length distribution the author measured in Chrome and other programs.
when_to_use: x86-64 code with AVX2 whose profile is dominated by short (0-512 byte), variable-length memset or memcpy calls you can route to a dedicated function, e.g. serialization, IPC message parsing, small-object zeroing.

As a reference design when writing your own short-size memset/memcpy: the size-class tree and overlapping-store tricks are easy to read and the repo's exhaustive tester (sizes 0-1023, all small offsets, guard bytes) is reusable.
If you already build Folly with AVX2 enabled: use __folly_memset (this memset plus a rep stosq path for fills of 4 KiB and up, licensed Apache-2.0) instead of the unlicensed original.
To find out whether your own program's calls are short enough to benefit, via the repo's LD_PRELOAD length-histogram tool.
when_not_to_use: Buffers above 511 bytes were never measured, and the code has no rep stosb/rep movsb, non-temporal store or prefetch path; for multi-kilobyte and larger fills or copies glibc's ERMS/non-temporal paths (and Folly's rep stosq branch, added when it upstreamed this memset) are the safer choice.

Overlapping buffers: asm_memcpy is plain memcpy and is not overlap-safe above 128 bytes, whereas glibc's x86-64 memcpy is its memmove entry (the README's own backtrace shows __memmove_avx_unaligned_erms) and Folly's memcpy detects overlap; swapping it in can expose latent overlap bugs.

CPUs without AVX2 (asm_memset uses vpbroadcastb; asm_memcpy needs AVX) or the Windows x64 ABI: there is no CPUID dispatch and the code assumes System V argument registers (rdi, rsi, rdx); Linux and macOS symbol variants only.
Anything that needs a license: the repository has no LICENSE file, so the code is all-rights-reserved reference material; only the memset has a licensed copy (Folly).
memcpy sizes of roughly 155-195 bytes (Folly faster) and 190-255 bytes (glibc called directly faster), as read from the author's own fixed-size chart (docs/memcpy_bench.png).

integration.form: source-drop (one .S file per function; harness built with CMake)
integration.dependencies: none for the functions; CMake 3.7+ and a C++14 compiler for the tester and benchmark
integration.min_toolchain: GNU as or clang's integrated assembler (AT&T syntax, C preprocessor for .S); harness C++14
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux and macOS, System V ABI; AVX2 required for memset, AVX for memcpy
integration.thread_safety: Reentrant: leaf functions with no global state (read from the source; not documented)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same signatures and return values as memset/memcpy but exported as asm_memset/asm_memcpy; no runtime dispatch, memcpy is not memmove-safe, and the repo's proxy shim forwards memset to the C local_memset, not the assembly

gotchas: Harness flaw in the headline 'random sizes' benchmark: offsets and sizes come from one fixed 320-byte table (include/utils.h DoomRNG) that is reset every sample; memset draws two bytes per call, so the same 160 (offset, size) pairs repeat 62,500 times in each 10M-call sample (memcpy draws three, a 320-call cycle). Branch predictors with long histories can learn much of a cycle that short, so the README's claim that this benchmark 'takes into account mispredicted branches' is optimistic; every implementation sees the same sequence, so the ranking is fair but the gap on genuinely random sizes is unmeasured. Hacker News commenters made the same priming criticism (search snippet of thread 29197161; the thread itself was not opened).

The 'musl' curve in the fixed-size memset chart is musl's portable C memset copied into src/memset/impl.c and compiled by the harness with -O3 -march=native, not the x86_64 assembly memset.s that musl actually ships (rep stosq above 126 bytes), so it does not represent musl libc on x86-64. 'libc' is &memset called directly and 'libc@plt' adds a jmp trampoline through the PLT; the direct column is the fair glibc comparison.

The README says the proxy tool swaps memset and memcpy, but src/memset/shims.c overrides only memset and forwards it to the C local_memset, not asm_memset; LD_PRELOAD experiments with it do not exercise the assembly.

The impl.S files carry no .note.GNU-stack section (nor .type/.size/CFI), so GNU ld marks a binary linking them as needing an executable stack; Folly fixed this in its copy (commit 0b150f5, #1814, 2022-07-11). Fixed-size sweeps use only 16-byte-aligned buffers at offset 0 with identical source and destination alignment.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it (or rather Folly's __folly_memset) over fancy-memset or Agner Fog's asmlib when the workload is short variable-length calls on AVX2 hardware and you want a tiny, readable size-class design; asmlib offers CPU dispatch and a full string-function set but its numbers are against glibc 2.7/2.8, and DPDK's rte_memcpy is the maintained, licensed choice for small cache-resident copies.
verified_claims_summary: On one unnamed AVX2 CPU with an unstated late-2021 glibc (issue #5 asking for both was never answered), the random-size benchmark (sizes and offsets 0-255, 10M calls, median of 20 samples, nop-call overhead subtracted) gives memset: glibc direct 20,172, via PLT 24,344, asm 14,295 (1.41x vs direct, derived from chart data); memcpy: glibc direct 25,263, Folly 23,969, asm 21,547 (1.17x, derived). The harness Stopwatch reports microseconds, so these read as about 2.0 vs 1.4 ns per memset call and 2.5 vs 2.2 ns per memcpy call (derived, assuming the charts plot the harness output); the only outside run (issue #6, 2023, Ivy Bridge i3-3210 without AVX2) timed the C huge_memset, not the assembly, and found musl faster.
status_note: Abandoned since 2022-01-10 (110 commits, 344 stars, 3 open issues unanswered) and unlicensed, so treat it as reference; the memset lives on, licensed and maintained, as folly/memset.S, while the memcpy was never upstreamed.
